text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: MAYA
text: Picture two portfolio companies owned by the same fund. One is a software business with two hundred engineers. The other runs four hundred HVAC technicians across three states. Which one has more to gain from AI this year?

speaker: GRANT
text: Most people would say the software company. And most people, I think, are wrong. The software company has already been told for three years that AI is its future. The HVAC business is still losing a quarter of its inbound calls to voicemail.

speaker: MAYA
text: Welcome to AI in the Real Economy, the show about AI value creation in the businesses that make, fix, deliver and care for things. I'm Maya.

speaker: GRANT
text: And I'm Grant. Over four episodes, we're going to look at services, healthcare, industrial and consumer businesses, the kinds of companies that make up most private equity portfolios, and ask where AI actually moves EBITDA. Everything we cite comes from public sources, and when a number comes from a vendor or a fund's own reporting, we'll say so.

speaker: MAYA
text: Let's start with the obvious objection. Isn't AI a technology story? Why would a fund look for it in a plumbing roll-up or a contract manufacturer?

speaker: GRANT
text: Because the value of AI shows up wherever there's a lot of repetitive judgment work done by people, and wherever revenue leaks because nobody had time to catch it. Non-software companies are full of both. Call centers. Dispatch desks. Estimating. Claims and billing. Quality inspection. Scheduling. Collections.

speaker: MAYA
text: And the labor market makes it urgent.

speaker: GRANT
text: It does. A Foley and Lardner piece from May this year on AI, automation and robotics in private equity singled out labor-constrained industries: logistics yards, food service, construction, field services and healthcare delivery. Places with labor shortages, wage inflation or big seasonal swings. In those businesses, AI isn't mainly about cutting people. It's about doing the work you can't hire for.

speaker: MAYA
text: There's also an exit argument.

speaker: GRANT
text: The same piece made it. With a tight exit environment and longer hold periods, value creation during the hold matters more. And they drew a useful distinction: one-time cost cuts tend to get competed away, while building AI into how the business operates gives you more durable margin. That's the story a buyer will pay for.

speaker: MAYA
text: Give me evidence that this is real and not just conference talk.

speaker: GRANT
text: Permira's a good example of a large fund that has talked publicly about it. In an interview with Private Equity International in September 2025, their team described AI value creation beyond the tech sector: in services, healthcare and consumer businesses, where AI is applied inside sector-specific workflows. Two of their portfolio examples stood out to me.

speaker: MAYA
text: Go on.

speaker: GRANT
text: In pharma services, they said AI in drug formulation cut a cycle from about ten weeks to four or five days. In clinical services, they said AI in adverse event case processing cut intake time by a quarter and improved auditability. Those are the fund's own numbers, so treat them as claims. But notice what they have in common. Neither is a chatbot bolted onto a website. Both sit inside the core work the customer pays for.

speaker: MAYA
text: And on the industrial side?

speaker: GRANT
text: Parsec Automation published a survey in July of twelve hundred manufacturing leaders. Seventy two percent said they had adopted AI in some form, up from fifty three percent in 2024. But only ten percent had deployed it across their operations. The top use cases were quality control, IT operations and supply chain management. The top barriers were implementation cost, data privacy and security, and integration with existing systems.

speaker: MAYA
text: So almost everyone has tried it, and almost nobody has scaled it.

speaker: GRANT
text: Which is exactly the gap a private equity owner is built to close. Funds are good at forcing a decision, funding it, and making management accountable for it.

speaker: MAYA
text: Let's give people a framework. When you walk into a non-software portfolio company, where do you look first?

speaker: GRANT
text: I use four levers. The first is revenue capture. Money the business has earned but doesn't collect. Missed calls, unquoted leads, under-billed jobs, denied claims, expired service agreements nobody renewed. AI is very good at catching leakage because it doesn't get tired at four on a Friday.

speaker: MAYA
text: Second.

speaker: GRANT
text: Labor leverage. Getting more output from the same people, especially scarce experts. A technician who spends forty minutes a day on paperwork. A nurse who spends an hour on notes after every shift. An estimator who builds every quote from scratch. You give that time back, and you've effectively hired without hiring.

speaker: MAYA
text: Third.

speaker: GRANT
text: Working capital. Faster invoicing, cleaner billing, fewer disputes, better inventory forecasts. This one's underrated, because it shows up in cash rather than EBITDA, and cash is what funds care about at exit.

speaker: MAYA
text: And fourth.

speaker: GRANT
text: Quality and risk. Fewer defects, fewer safety incidents, fewer compliance misses, better documentation. It's harder to put a number on, but it protects the multiple. A buyer's diligence team will find the defects and the compliance gaps either way.

speaker: MAYA
text: Which lever usually pays first?

speaker: GRANT
text: Revenue capture, almost every time. It's measurable within weeks, it doesn't require anyone to change their job, and it funds the harder work.

speaker: MAYA
text: Now the failure modes. Because I've seen a lot of real-economy AI programs stall.

speaker: GRANT
text: Three big ones. The first is pilot sprawl. Every site manager tries a different tool, nothing connects to the system of record, and after a year you have twelve pilots and no EBITDA. The fix is to pick a small number of workflows and run them across the whole business.

speaker: MAYA
text: Second.

speaker: GRANT
text: Treating AI as an IT project. Permira's team said every portfolio company should have a chief AI officer or equivalent on the management team, not tucked away in IT. I'd put it more simply. The person who owns the workflow has to own the AI in that workflow. If dispatch is the use case, the head of operations owns it.

speaker: MAYA
text: And third.

speaker: GRANT
text: Ignoring the people doing the work. In a services business, the technicians and the call center staff decide whether AI works. If they see it as a threat, they'll route around it. If they see it as taking the worst parts of their day away, they'll make it better. Change management isn't a soft add-on here. It's the plan.

speaker: MAYA
text: So where are we going over the next three episodes?

speaker: GRANT
text: Episode two is services: field services, home services and business services, and the AI-enabled roll-up thesis that a lot of funds are chasing. Episode three is healthcare services and other regulated work, where documentation and compliance shape what's possible. And episode four is factories and franchises, plus a hundred-day plan that a fund could actually run.

speaker: MAYA
text: And the thread through all of it?

speaker: GRANT
text: Start where the money leaks, put AI inside the core workflow, make the workflow owner accountable, and measure it in dollars, not demos.
[OUTRO MUSIC]

speaker: MAYA
text: Thanks for listening to AI in the Real Economy. I'm Maya.

speaker: GRANT
text: And I'm Grant. See you next time.
